- Early in the illness routine studies can be normal, so a normal test does not exclude botulism.

## Separating the look-alikes
- **Lambert-Eaton syndrome** is also presynaptic (antibodies to the calcium channel) and gives the same pattern with a much larger increment, typically above 100%. Clinically it is subacute, proximal, with absent reflexes that return after exercise, and often with small-cell lung cancer.
- **Myasthenia gravis**: decrement at slow rates, normal pupils, fatigable weakness.
- **Guillain-Barré syndrome and its Miller Fisher variant**: a nerve disease, so conduction is slowed or blocked, F waves are abnormal, there are sensory symptoms and CSF protein is raised. Classical Guillain-Barré ascends; Miller Fisher descends and is the closest clinical mimic of botulism.

options.A: A decrement at slow rates is the classic finding of myasthenia gravis. It may appear in botulism but is inconsistent and does not point to it.
options.B: Correct. An increment with fast stimulation marks a presynaptic release defect; with fixed pupils, descending weakness and normal sensation, that is botulism.
options.C: Sensory conduction is normal in botulism. Slowing indicates a neuropathy such as Guillain-Barré syndrome, and the stem states that sensation is intact.
options.D: Fibrillations indicate axonal or motor neuron damage. They can appear late in severe botulism, when muscle fibres have been cut off from their nerve for weeks, but they are not the finding that supports the diagnosis.

31.picks_note: Your pick, A, is the right test read from the wrong side of the junction: a decrement at slow rates means a postsynaptic disorder (myasthenia), and the fixed pupils in the stem exclude myasthenia, which never involves the pupil. HT picked D: denervation potentials indicate disease of the nerve or motor neuron, whereas the stem's normal conduction and intact sensation place the lesion at the junction.

key.note: Textbooks, including Irwin & Rippe, quote 20 to 50 Hz (or post-exercise facilitation) for the incremental response; the exact rate does not change the answer.

35.answer: B. Start TB therapy plus steroids.
35.why: Basal meningitis with lymphocytic, low-glucose CSF, upper-lobe lung opacities and failure of antibacterial treatment is tuberculous meningitis until proved otherwise. Outcome depends on how early treatment begins, and the tests are slow and insensitive, so anti-tuberculous therapy is started on clinical probability once samples have been sent. Dexamethasone is started with it because it reduces deaths.
35.watch: 'Wait for CSF culture' sounds careful, but culture takes weeks and is positive in fewer than half of cases, and a negative smear or molecular test does not exclude the disease. She is already obtunded, and treatment started after coma sets in has a far worse result.
35.hook: In probable TB meningitis, send the samples, then treat with four drugs and dexamethasone the same day. Confirmation follows treatment.
35.explain:
## Why the steroid is part of the answer
Your card CNS-27 has the CSF findings, the drug regimen and the dexamethasone dose and taper. What this question adds is the reasoning.

The harm in tuberculous meningitis comes less from the bacilli than from the thick inflammatory exudate they provoke at the base of the brain. It surrounds the cranial nerves (palsies), blocks CSF flow (hydrocephalus) and inflames the arteries passing through it (infarcts, typically in the basal ganglia). Starting treatment can briefly increase this inflammation as bacilli die. Dexamethasone damps it. In the trial that settled the question (Thwaites, Vietnam, 2004) it reduced mortality, although it did not reduce disability among survivors.

## Why not wait
CSF smear is positive in a small minority, culture needs two to six weeks, and molecular tests, even Xpert Ultra, miss a meaningful share of cases, so none can be used to rule the disease out. A large volume of CSF improves the yield. The stage at which treatment begins is the strongest predictor of outcome: good when the patient is alert, poor once in coma.

Deterioration on treatment should prompt imaging for hydrocephalus, which may need CSF diversion, and a sodium level, since hyponatraemia is common.

options.A: Corticosteroids lower mortality in tuberculous meningitis. They are added, not stopped.
options.B: Correct. Empirical four-drug therapy with adjunctive dexamethasone, started once samples are sent.
options.C: Culture takes weeks and is negative in more than half of true cases. Waiting in a deteriorating patient costs brain.
options.D: Antibacterial cover has already failed, and the picture (lymphocytes, low glucose, basal disease, upper-lobe opacities) is tuberculous.

36.why: She is worsening clinically and on imaging while her microbiology improves, and the worsening began after antiretroviral therapy was started. That combination defines paradoxical immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS). The recovering immune system mounts a strong inflammatory response to mycobacterial antigens that are still present in her tissues, even though the bacilli are dying.
36.watch: Multidrug-resistant tuberculosis is the alternative that must always be considered when a patient deteriorates on treatment. Here the stem excludes it with two words, 'microbiologic improvement': resistant disease stays culture-positive.
36.hook: Worse on the scan, better on the cultures, soon after starting ART: this is the immune system returning, not the treatment failing.
36.explain:
## What is happening
In advanced HIV there are too few CD4 cells to form granulomas or to produce much inflammation, so tuberculosis can be widespread and yet clinically quiet. Antiretroviral therapy (ART) lowers the viral load within weeks, and functioning T cells return. They find a large amount of mycobacterial antigen, alive or dead, and respond to it vigorously. The inflammation, not the infection, produces the new fever, enlarging and sometimes suppurating lymph nodes, worsening lung infiltrates, effusions, and enlarging tuberculomas in the brain.

## Two forms
- **Paradoxical IRIS**: tuberculosis already diagnosed and improving on treatment, then worsening after ART begins. This patient.
- **Unmasking IRIS**: tuberculosis that was present but unrecognised declares itself, often dramatically, in the first weeks of ART.

## Who gets it and when
It typically begins one to four weeks after ART is started, and nearly always within three months. The risks are a low CD4 count (below 50 to 100 cells/µL), a high viral load, disseminated or extrapulmonary tuberculosis, and a short interval between starting tuberculosis treatment and starting ART.

## Diagnosis and management
It is a diagnosis of exclusion. Drug resistance, poor adherence, drug toxicity and a second opportunistic infection must be looked for first.

- Tuberculosis treatment and ART are both continued. ART is interrupted only if the reaction is life-threatening, which mainly means disease in the central nervous system.
- Mild cases receive anti-inflammatory drugs. Moderate or severe cases receive prednisolone, 1.5 mg/kg/day for two weeks and then 0.75 mg/kg/day for two weeks.
- Prevention: in patients with a CD4 count of 100 or below who start ART within a month of tuberculosis treatment, prophylactic prednisone (40 mg daily for two weeks, then 20 mg daily for two weeks) lowered the incidence of IRIS in the PredART trial.

## Timing of ART, the usual companion question
WHO advises starting ART within two weeks of starting tuberculosis treatment whatever the CD4 count, because the survival gain from early ART outweighs the risk of IRIS. Tuberculous meningitis is the exception: ART is delayed for at least four weeks and started within eight, because IRIS inside the skull can kill. Cryptococcal meningitis is handled the same way, with ART delayed four to six weeks.

options.A: Resistant disease would remain smear or culture positive. The stem states microbiological improvement.
options.B: Drug toxicity could explain lung changes but not enlarging intracranial lesions, and it has no link to the timing of ART.
options.C: Correct. Paradoxical worsening at known sites of tuberculosis after ART, with improving microbiology, is IRIS.
options.D: A bacterial pneumonia could explain fever and a new infiltrate, but not the growth of lesions in the brain.

38.why: The stem is dated by the neutrophil count, not by a day number. An ANC of 650/μL that is rising means the graft has just taken (engraftment is an ANC above 500/μL), and fever, rash, hypoxaemia and diffuse infiltrates appearing in that same window, with no infection, are engraftment syndrome. The returning neutrophils and the cytokines released with them make capillaries leak in the skin and the lung.
38.watch: Idiopathic pneumonia syndrome also gives diffuse infiltrates without infection, but it comes weeks later, has no rash and no link to the day the count recovers, and it responds poorly to steroids. The rash plus the rising ANC is what separates the two.
38.hook: Fever, rash and wet lungs on the days the neutrophils come back: engraftment syndrome, and it melts with a short steroid course.
38.explain:
## What your cards leave to add
Your transplant timeline cards place engraftment syndrome in the peri-engraftment slot and say it responds well to steroids. Three details are worth adding because they are what this question and its GT 8 twin test.

First, the definition is tied to the count. The usual (Spitzer) criteria ask for the picture to appear within 96 hours of engraftment, engraftment being an ANC above 500/μL, and need three major features or two major plus one minor. The major features are a non-infectious fever, an erythematous rash over more than a quarter of the body, and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema with hypoxaemia; the minor ones are weight gain, liver or kidney dysfunction and a transient encephalopathy. The looser Maiolino criteria accept a non-infectious fever plus any one of rash, pulmonary infiltrates or diarrhoea, from 24 hours before neutrophil recovery onwards.

Second, it is commoner after autologous than allogeneic transplant, and after growth-factor (G-CSF) use, although this stem happens to describe an allogeneic recipient.

Third, treatment is a short course of systemic corticosteroid, usually only a few days, once infection has been looked for; mild cases settle with supportive care and diuretics alone.

The near neighbour that also arrives around engraftment is diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, recognised by lavage fluid that becomes bloodier with each aliquot rather than by a rash.

options.A: Bronchiolitis obliterans syndrome is the lung form of chronic graft-versus-host disease. It appears after day 100 with fixed airflow obstruction and air trapping, a clear chest film, and no fever or rash.
options.B: Organising pneumonia is a late complication with patchy peripheral consolidation and a restrictive defect. It is unrelated to neutrophil recovery.
options.C: Correct. Fever, rash and non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within days of the ANC crossing 500/μL.
options.D: Idiopathic pneumonia syndrome is diffuse non-infectious lung injury in the first four months, usually weeks after engraftment, without a rash and with a poor steroid response.

41.why: Dynamic airway collapse happens when, during expiration, the pressure inside a small airway falls below the pleural pressure squeezing it from outside. The only way to stop it is to raise the pressure inside the airway during expiration. Pursed lips do exactly that: they add a resistance at the mouth, so pressure stays higher all the way back up the airway and the collapsible segment is held open.
41.watch: Shortening inspiratory time (the option you both chose) gives more time to breathe out, which reduces air trapping, but it does nothing to the pressure inside the airway, so the airway still collapses at the same point. More time through a collapsed tube is not the same as an open tube.
41.hook: A collapsing airway needs back-pressure from downstream, not more time: pursed lips in the awake patient, external PEEP on the ventilator.
41.explain:
## Why the airway collapses
Air leaves the alveolus because alveolar pressure is higher than mouth pressure. Alveolar pressure is the sum of two things: pleural pressure and the elastic recoil of the lung. As air travels towards the mouth, friction uses up pressure, so the pressure inside the airway falls steadily along its length. At some point it has fallen by exactly the amount of the recoil pressure, and there the pressure inside the airway equals pleural pressure outside it. This is the equal pressure point. Downstream of it (towards the mouth) the outside pressure is higher and the airway is compressed.

In a healthy lung the equal pressure point sits in the large airways, which have cartilage and do not collapse. Emphysema moves it into the small, unsupported airways for two reasons: destroyed elastic tissue means low recoil, so there is less pressure to lose before the point is reached, and narrowed airways mean pressure is lost faster. The harder the patient pushes, the higher the pleural pressure and the tighter the squeeze, so extra effort produces no extra flow. That is expiratory flow limitation, and the gas left behind is dynamic hyperinflation and auto-PEEP.

## Why back-pressure works
A resistance at the mouth raises the pressure in every airway upstream of it. The equal pressure point moves back towards the mouth, into airways that can resist compression. Flow is slower but continues for the whole of expiration, so the lung empties further.

## The ventilator version
An intubated patient cannot purse his lips, so the stem is loosely written; the principle is what is being tested. On the ventilator the same job is done by external PEEP, set to about 80% of the measured auto-PEEP, which holds flow-limited airways open and lowers the effort needed to trigger without adding to hyperinflation (the waterfall effect on your linked card). The old expiratory retard setting was the direct mechanical copy of pursed lips.

## What actually reduces trapping
These are a different question from what stops collapse: lower respiratory rate (the most effective single change), smaller tidal volume, higher inspiratory flow to shorten inspiration, and bronchodilators.

options.A: Higher inspiratory pressure delivers a bigger breath into an already over-filled lung. It acts in inspiration and worsens hyperinflation.
options.B: Correct. Expiratory back-pressure keeps intraluminal pressure above pleural pressure and splints the airway open.
options.C: A smaller tidal volume leaves less to exhale and so reduces trapping, but the airway still collapses at the same point during expiration.
options.D: A shorter inspiratory time lengthens expiration and reduces trapping. It does not raise airway pressure during expiration, so it does not prevent collapse.

41.picks_note: You and HT both picked D. It looked right because shortening inspiration is a real, standard manoeuvre for air trapping. The stem, however, asks what reduces airway collapse, and only an option that raises expiratory airway pressure does that.

key.note: The stem describes a ventilated patient, who cannot purse his lips. B is still the only option that raises expiratory airway pressure; the ventilator equivalent is external PEEP.

43.why: PEEP raises intrathoracic pressure, which raises right atrial pressure and so reduces the pressure gradient driving venous blood back to the chest. Less blood reaches the right heart, then the lungs, then the left ventricle. Left-sided filling pressure falls, pulmonary capillary pressure falls with it, and less fluid is pushed into the alveoli. The stem names this itself: congestion improves alongside a fall in venous return.
43.watch: PEEP lowers left ventricular afterload; it never raises it. Option A has the right variable with the wrong direction.
43.hook: Positive pressure helps the failing left ventricle twice, less blood coming in and less wall tension pushing out, and this stem asks about the first.
43.explain:
## Completing the picture on your cards
Your heart-lung interaction card traces a positive-pressure breath, and your cardiogenic shock card states that positive pressure has a net positive effect on the left ventricle. What links them is why a fall in venous return, which would drop cardiac output in a normal or hypovolaemic patient, is harmless or helpful here.

A failing, overfilled ventricle is working on the flat part of its Starling curve. Removing some preload hardly changes stroke volume, but it does lower the filling pressure that is flooding the lung. The same ventricle is very sensitive to afterload. Afterload is the wall tension needed to eject, and it depends on the pressure across the ventricular wall (pressure inside minus pleural pressure outside). Raising pleural pressure with PEEP reduces that difference, so the ventricle ejects more easily. In the lung, PEEP also reopens flooded alveoli and takes over the work of breathing, which cuts oxygen demand.

The reverse happens when positive pressure is removed, which is weaning-induced pulmonary oedema on your third linked card.

In acute cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, CPAP or NIV improves breathlessness and gas exchange faster than oxygen alone; the 3CPO trial found no difference in mortality.

options.A: Wrong direction. Raised pleural pressure lowers the pressure across the left ventricular wall, so afterload falls.
options.B: Correct. Lower venous return lowers left-sided filling pressure and pulmonary capillary pressure.
options.C: PEEP and ventilatory support reduce the work of breathing and wall tension, so myocardial oxygen demand falls.
options.D: Right ventricular preload falls, because venous return to the chest is reduced.

43.picks_note: HT picked A. Afterload is indeed part of how PEEP helps the left ventricle, which is why the option attracts, but the change is a decrease, and the stem's own clue (reduced venous return) points to preload.

45.why: The timing gives the answer. Bright haemoptysis and collapse within moments of inflating the balloon mean the balloon has torn the vessel it was sitting in. This happens when the tip has drifted into a small distal branch, so the full 1.5 mL stretches a vessel too narrow to take it, or when the balloon is inflated against resistance.
45.watch: Pulmonary infarction also comes from the catheter sitting too far out, but it follows prolonged wedging or a clot around the tip and develops over hours with pleuritic pain and a wedge-shaped shadow. It does not announce itself at the instant of inflation.
45.hook: Haemoptysis at the moment the balloon goes up is a torn pulmonary artery until proved otherwise.
45.explain:
## Beyond the complications card
Your card lists the risk factors (pulmonary hypertension, age, anticoagulation, a distal tip, over-inflation) and the figures: rare, at 0.03-0.2%, but fatal in roughly half. Two things it does not carry are how to respond and how to prevent it.

## Immediate management
The danger is drowning of the good lung, so the first moves protect it. Turn the patient with the bleeding side down (usually the right, since most catheters float into the right pulmonary artery). Secure the airway and isolate the lungs, either by advancing a single-lumen tube into the opposite main bronchus or with a double-lumen tube or bronchial blocker. Apply PEEP, which helps tamponade the bleeding vessel, and reverse any anticoagulation. Do not simply pull the catheter out: it is usually withdrawn a few centimetres with the balloon down, and many texts then re-inflate the balloon to occlude the feeding artery. Definitive control is by angiographic embolisation or surgical resection. A patient who survives may have formed a false aneurysm that bleeds again days later, so imaging follows.

## Prevention, which is the more likely exam question
- Inflate slowly while watching the trace and stop as soon as the wedge waveform appears; never exceed 1.5 mL.
- If the trace wedges with much less than the full volume, the tip is too distal; pull it back.
- Keep each wedge brief, a few breaths at most, and limit how often it is done.
- Deflate before any withdrawal, and never flush the catheter while it is wedged.
- In pulmonary hypertension use the pulmonary artery diastolic pressure as the estimate instead of repeated wedging.

options.A: Infarction follows prolonged wedging or thrombosis around a distal tip. It evolves over hours and does not cause sudden massive haemoptysis at inflation.
options.B: Air embolism belongs to insertion or an open hub, or to a burst balloon in a patient with a right-to-left shunt. It does not cause haemoptysis.
options.C: Correct. Balloon inflation in a distal branch tears the vessel: haemoptysis, hypoxaemia and collapse at once.
options.D: Knotting comes from coiling in the right ventricle during repeated passes. The problem it causes is a catheter that will not come out.

47.why: In metabolic acidosis the lungs are the compensation: deep, fast breathing blows off carbon dioxide and holds the pH up. That breathing is muscular work, and it cannot be kept up indefinitely. The ventilator is started to carry that work when the muscles are about to fail, so that the low PaCO2 is maintained while insulin and fluids remove the acid. It treats the pump, not the acidosis.
47.watch: Option A sounds like the purpose but is not. A ventilator can only change PaCO2; the keto-acids are still there. Correcting the metabolic acidosis is the job of insulin and fluids.
47.hook: In DKA the ventilator is there to keep doing what the tiring respiratory muscles were doing, at the same minute ventilation, and nothing more.
47.explain:
## What the numbers in the stem already show
For a bicarbonate of 14, full respiratory compensation predicts a PaCO2 of about 29 mmHg (Winter's formula: 1.5 x 14 + 8). If the PaCO2 were 29 the pH would be about 7.30. The stem gives pH 7.08, and working backwards from that pH and bicarbonate the PaCO2 must be near 48 mmHg. So this patient is no longer compensating: a respiratory acidosis from failing muscles is already sitting on top of the metabolic one. That is the fatigue the question is pointing at, and it explains why the pH is so much worse than the bicarbonate alone would suggest.

## Why the muscles fail
Kussmaul breathing can multiply minute ventilation several-fold. The respiratory muscles, which normally take under 5% of the body's oxygen consumption, may then take a quarter or more, at a time when dehydration has reduced the cardiac output that supplies them and acidosis itself weakens muscle contraction. Demand exceeds supply. The signs are a rising respiratory rate with falling tidal volume, accessory muscle use, paradoxical abdominal movement and finally a PaCO2 that starts to climb.

## The danger at intubation
This is the part most likely to be asked next. Once sedated and paralysed the patient stops hyperventilating. If PaCO2 rises from 25 to 40 mmHg during the apnoea of induction or on ordinary ventilator settings, at a bicarbonate of 14 the pH falls by about 0.2 within minutes, enough to precipitate cardiac arrest. Therefore:

- intubate only when it is truly needed, and keep ventilating through induction rather than allowing a long apnoeic pause;
- set the ventilator to reproduce the patient's own high minute ventilation (large rate, adequate tidal volume) and aim for the PaCO2 that Winter's formula predicts, not for 40;
- check a blood gas early and watch for air trapping at high rates.

## Bicarbonate
Bicarbonate has no routine place in DKA. Guidelines reserve it for a pH below about 7.0 (older text: below 6.9), because it can cause hypokalaemia, paradoxical intracellular and cerebral acidosis, and slower ketone clearance.

options.A: The ventilator controls PaCO2 only. The acid load is cleared by insulin, fluids and the kidney.
options.B: Correct. Ventilation takes over the work of compensatory hyperventilation before the muscles fail and PaCO2 rises.
options.C: Ventilation and bicarbonate are separate decisions; one does not remove the need to consider the other.
options.D: Lactate is not the problem in DKA, and ventilation does not act on its production except indirectly by resting the muscles.

48.why: This patient's oxygenation depends on a PEEP of 14 holding unstable alveoli open. Open suctioning means disconnecting the circuit, and the moment that happens airway pressure falls to zero, the recruited alveoli collapse, and suction then pulls more gas out of the lung. A closed (in-line) catheter sits inside a sleeve within the circuit and is advanced through a sealed port, so ventilation, PEEP and oxygen continue throughout. The repeated desaturations in the stem are the sign that disconnection is the problem.
48.watch: Closed suction is chosen to protect lung volume and oxygenation. It has not been shown to reduce ventilator-associated pneumonia, so do not pick it for that reason.
48.hook: If the lung is being held open by PEEP, do not open the circuit to suction it.
48.explain:
## Why disconnection costs so much in ARDS
In ARDS the surfactant is damaged and the lung is heavy with oedema, so many alveoli stay open only because end-expiratory pressure is splinting them. They collapse within seconds of losing that pressure, and re-opening them needs a higher pressure and more time than keeping them open did. One disconnection can therefore cost many minutes of poor oxygenation, and each collapse and re-opening adds shear injury. Suction makes it worse by applying negative pressure and removing oxygen-rich gas. The loss of intrathoracic pressure also swings venous return and blood pressure.

## When a closed system is the right choice
The textbook thresholds, which are what this bank uses, are PEEP above 10 cmH2O, FiO2 above 0.6, or a high mean airway pressure. Other standard indications are desaturation or haemodynamic instability on disconnection, an infection spread by the airborne route (tuberculosis, respiratory viruses), and inhaled gases such as nitric oxide that should not be interrupted. The 2022 AARC guideline states that either an open or a closed system can be used safely and effectively in adults generally, so the choice is made on these grounds, not as a universal rule.

## Suctioning technique an examiner can ask
- Suction only when needed (visible or audible secretions, a saw-tooth flow trace, rising peak pressure), not on a schedule.
- Preoxygenate before suctioning; 100% is not obligatory, and an FiO2 about 0.2 above baseline may be enough.
- Each pass lasts no more than 15 seconds.
- The catheter should occlude less than half of the tube lumen in adults and children (under 70% in neonates).
- Keep suction pressure below 200 mmHg (negative) in adults and below 120 mmHg in children; older texts quote 100-150 mmHg for adults.
- Do not instil saline routinely.

Complications to recognise are hypoxaemia, atelectasis, bradycardia from vagal stimulation, mucosal trauma and a rise in intracranial pressure.

options.A: Open suction requires disconnection, which removes PEEP and causes derecruitment and desaturation, the very problem described.
options.B: A Yankauer sucker clears the mouth and oropharynx. It cannot reach the trachea through an endotracheal tube.
options.C: Correct. The in-line catheter preserves PEEP, oxygen delivery and ventilation during suctioning.
options.D: Removing the tube to suction abandons the airway in a patient who is dependent on high PEEP and oxygen.

49.why: An aerosol reaches the lung only if a large enough breath carries it past the circuit and tube, slowly enough that the droplets do not hit the walls. Volume control guarantees the tidal volume on every breath whatever the airway resistance. In pressure control the tidal volume depends on the patient's mechanics, and in severe asthma high resistance makes it small and variable, so less drug is carried in and the dose is unpredictable. This is the textbook statement (Pilbeam) the item is built on, and the one scintigraphy trial that compared modes found higher lung deposition with volume control (15% against 10.5% of the dose with pressure support, in 17 patients).
49.watch: A square (constant) flow waveform is what you set to ventilate an asthmatic, because it shortens inspiration; the textbook this bank follows says it delivers less aerosol than a decelerating or sine pattern. Do not choose a setting because it is right for the asthma; the question asks only about drug delivery.
49.hook: Aerosol wants a guaranteed, large, slow breath; of these four options only volume control promises the volume.
49.explain:
## How an aerosol gets lost
Droplets of 1-5 micrometres are the ones that reach small airways. On a ventilator they must travel through tubing, a Y-piece and a narrow endotracheal tube first, and at each bend or narrowing a fast-moving droplet leaves the airstream and sticks to the wall (impaction). Warm, humid gas makes droplets swell, so more of them are lost. Only a minority of the nominal dose reaches the lung, often around 10-15% even with a good set-up, which is why doses for ventilated patients are higher than for ambulant ones.

## The textbook settings (what this bank tests)
Standard texts list the ventilator factors that favour delivery, all following from that picture: a guaranteed tidal volume large enough to clear the circuit dead space (volume control), a slow inspiratory flow with a longer inspiratory time, a lower respiratory rate, and a non-square flow pattern. Expect these as keys.

## The device and the circuit (current guidance)
The 2023 international consensus on aerosol therapy in critically ill adults (Annals of Intensive Care) recommends:

- A vibrating-mesh nebuliser or a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer, with no preference between the two. A continuous jet nebuliser is not preferred: it is less efficient and its driving gas alters tidal volume, flow and FiO2.
- With bias flow in the circuit, place the nebuliser in the inspiratory limb towards the ventilator, away from the Y-piece.
- An inhaler goes through a spacer of more than 150 mL in the inspiratory limb, fired at the start of inspiration, puffs at least 15 seconds apart.
- Remove or bypass a heat-moisture exchanger, which can cut the delivered dose to almost nothing. Heated humidification reduces delivery by up to half in bench tests, but the humidifier is not switched off for routine treatments.
- Do not change the mode, the ventilator settings or the tube size, and do not use heliox, solely to improve aerosol delivery; the evidence on mode is mixed.

## Putting the two together
The question asks which setting delivers most, and on that the textbook and the small trial agree on volume control. In practice the guideline answer is to get the device and circuit right and leave the ventilator set for the asthma.

options.A: In pressure control the tidal volume varies with resistance and compliance. In severe bronchospasm it falls, so drug delivery is lower and less predictable.
options.B: A high rate shortens inspiratory time and each breath carries less aerosol to the lower airways; in asthma it also worsens air trapping.
options.C: Correct. A fixed tidal volume on every breath gives the most consistent transport of aerosol into the lung.
options.D: Per the textbook this bank follows, a square waveform delivers less aerosol than a decelerating or sine pattern, because constant high flow increases impaction. Bench data with mesh nebulisers are mixed.

49.picks_note: Your pick, A, was reasonable: pressure control gives a decelerating flow, which the textbook counts in favour of deposition. What rules it out is the patient: in status asthmaticus pressure control cannot guarantee the volume that carries the drug. HT picked D, probably because a square waveform is the usual asthma setting; it is chosen there to lengthen expiration and it reduces aerosol delivery.

key.note: Follows Pilbeam. The only in-vivo comparison (17 patients) supports volume control, but the 2023 consensus finds the evidence on mode mixed and advises against changing mode solely for aerosol delivery. If an item offers the device (mesh nebuliser or spacer) or HME removal, those are the better-established answers.

51.why: A closed anion gap means the keto-acid anions have gone, so the ketoacidosis itself is over. The bicarbonate is still low because the body has not yet rebuilt it, and chloride from the saline has taken the place the ketone anions used to occupy. A low bicarbonate with a normal gap is, by definition, a hyperchloraemic normal-gap acidosis, and after twelve hours of DKA treatment it is expected.
51.watch: Lactate, methanol and sulfate are all unmeasured anions. Each would hold the gap open, so a normal gap excludes all three at once.
51.hook: Gap closed but bicarbonate still low after DKA treatment is the hyperchloraemic tail of recovery, not treatment failure.
51.explain:
## Why bicarbonate lags behind
Your DKA card already states the sequence (high gap at presentation, hyperchloraemic normal gap in recovery) and gives saline chloride and renal bicarbonate loss as the reasons. The step worth understanding is what 'renal bicarbonate loss' means here, because no bicarbonate is actually seen in the urine.

Every ketone anion in the blood stands for one bicarbonate that was used up buffering its hydrogen ion. When insulin is given, the liver metabolises those anions and each one regenerates a bicarbonate, so they are sometimes called potential bicarbonate. A patient with good kidneys and a brisk diuresis, however, passes a large share of the ketone anions into the urine as sodium and potassium salts before insulin arrives. Those are lost for good, and the bicarbonate they would have regenerated is lost with them. Saline then replaces the missing anion with chloride.

The kidney repairs the deficit over the next day or two by excreting acid as ammonium. No specific treatment is needed. Do not keep the insulin infusion running to chase the bicarbonate once ketones have cleared, and note that balanced crystalloids produce less of this than 0.9% saline. For the same reason current guidance judges resolution by ketones and pH, not by the bicarbonate alone.

options.A: Lactic acidosis adds lactate, an unmeasured anion, and the gap would still be raised.
options.B: Correct. Ketone anions lost in urine plus chloride from saline leave a normal-gap, hyperchloraemic acidosis during recovery.
options.C: Methanol is metabolised to formate, which raises the anion gap (and early on the osmolal gap).
options.D: Sulfate retention is a cause of the high-gap acidosis of advanced renal failure.

52.why: Fluid from the small bowel, pancreas and bile is rich in bicarbonate, and diarrhoea carries it out of the body. No new acid anion has been added to the blood; bicarbonate has simply been removed, and the kidney retains chloride to keep the charges balanced. Bicarbonate falls, chloride rises by the same amount, and the anion gap stays normal.
52.watch: The other three options all add an anion that the gap formula does not measure, so each gives a high gap. The single phrase 'normal anion gap' removes them.
52.hook: Normal gap means bicarbonate was lost and chloride filled the space; high gap means an acid was added.
52.explain:
## Using the gap as the sorting step
Your cards carry the two lists. The reasoning that makes the lists unnecessary in a question like this is one step: the anion gap rises only when an acid arrives with an anion other than chloride. Phosphate and sulfate (retained in advanced renal failure), salicylate, and the glycolate and oxalate formed from ethylene glycol are all such anions. Diarrhoea adds none.

Two neighbouring points are commonly asked from the same stem. First, chronic diarrhoea also loses potassium, so the weakness here is hypokalaemia, and this is a normal-gap acidosis with low potassium, as are renal tubular acidosis types 1 and 2. Second, to tell a gut cause from a renal one, use the urine anion gap (urine sodium plus potassium minus chloride). A healthy kidney responds to acidosis by excreting ammonium chloride, so in diarrhoea the urine gap is negative; in distal renal tubular acidosis the kidney cannot do this and the gap is positive.

A caution on option B: early chronic kidney disease can produce a normal-gap acidosis because ammonium production falls, but phosphate retention specifically belongs to late disease and a high gap.

options.A: Correct. Bicarbonate-rich intestinal fluid is lost and chloride is retained: hyperchloraemic, normal-gap acidosis.
options.B: Phosphate is an unmeasured anion retained in advanced renal failure, giving a high-gap acidosis.
options.C: Salicylate poisoning gives a high-gap metabolic acidosis together with a respiratory alkalosis.
options.D: Ethylene glycol is metabolised to glycolic and oxalic acids: high anion gap, with a raised osmolal gap early.

52.picks_note: HT picked B. Renal failure is a genuine cause of metabolic acidosis in a 67-year-old, which is the pull, but retained phosphate widens the gap, and the stem gives both a normal gap and chronic diarrhoea.

53.why: Toxic megacolon is the end of the line for a severe colitis: the inflammation is no longer confined to the mucosa but has gone through the full thickness of the wall. What the endoscope sees is the surface of that process, which is widespread deep ulceration with mucosa so inflamed that it bleeds on the lightest touch (friable) or spontaneously. The bleeding in the stem comes from that surface.
53.watch: Aphthous ulcers are small, shallow, punched-out ulcers on otherwise normal-looking mucosa, the earliest lesion of Crohn's disease. They mark mild, early disease and are the opposite end of the spectrum from this patient.
53.hook: Toxic megacolon is transmural colitis, so its mucosa is deeply ulcerated and bleeds on contact; and the scope that shows it can also perforate it.
53.explain:
## What toxic megacolon is
In ordinary colitis the inflammation stays in the mucosa. When it extends into the muscle layer, inflammatory cells release nitric oxide, which paralyses the smooth muscle, and the nerve plexus is damaged. The colon stops contracting and dilates, its thinned wall lets bacteria and toxins through, and the patient becomes septic. The definition therefore has two halves: a colon dilated beyond 6 cm on imaging, and systemic toxicity by Jalan's criteria (on your linked card). The usual causes are ulcerative colitis, C. difficile and other infective colitis, and cytomegalovirus in the immunosuppressed. Hypokalaemia, opioids, anticholinergics, antidiarrhoeal drugs and barium studies can tip a severe colitis into it.

## What the endoscope shows
Severe colitis loses its normal vascular pattern first (oedema hides the vessels), then becomes granular and friable, then ulcerates. At the fulminant end there are extensive, deep ulcers with spontaneous bleeding. If the cause is C. difficile, the finding to remember instead is pseudomembranes: raised yellow-white plaques on the mucosa.

## The practical caution
Full colonoscopy and bowel preparation are generally avoided in toxic megacolon, because insufflating a paper-thin colon can perforate it. If tissue or a look is essential, a limited sigmoidoscopy without preparation and with minimal air is done. The question accepts the colonoscopy as given, so answer the finding, but know that an item asking for the investigation of choice wants CT (or a plain film for the diameter), not endoscopy.

## Management in outline
Nil by mouth, nasogastric decompression, fluid and potassium replacement, stopping the precipitating drugs, antibiotics, and treatment of the cause (intravenous steroids for ulcerative colitis; vancomycin and metronidazole for C. difficile). Surgery, a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy, is needed for perforation, uncontrolled bleeding, progressive dilatation, or failure to improve within about 48-72 hours.

options.A: Aphthous ulcers are shallow and discrete, typical of early Crohn's disease, not of fulminant colitis.
options.B: Correct. Deep, widespread ulceration with friable, bleeding mucosa reflects severe transmural inflammation.
options.C: The vascular pattern is lost early in any active colitis, so a normal pattern excludes severe disease.
options.D: Polyps are not a feature. Inflammatory pseudopolyps may be seen in long-standing colitis but do not define severity.

53.picks_note: HT picked A (a guess). An ulcer of any kind sounds like colitis, but 'superficial' is the word that excludes it: toxic megacolon implies deep, full-thickness disease. You left this one blank.

key.note: The finding is right, but the premise is unusual: colonoscopy is normally avoided in toxic megacolon because of perforation risk.

54.why: Lactescent serum is serum turned milky by chylomicrons, the triglyceride-carrying particles, and it appears only when triglycerides are very high. Triglycerides above about 1,000 mg/dL are themselves a cause of pancreatitis, so in this stem the lipid result is the aetiology and not a side effect. The hyperglycaemia fits as well, since poorly controlled diabetes is the commonest reason for triglycerides to reach that level.
54.watch: Alcohol also raises triglycerides and can make serum lipaemic, which is why option A is there. The rise with alcohol is usually moderate; a marked elevation with milky serum points to a primary lipid disorder as the cause.
54.hook: Milky serum in pancreatitis means triglycerides above 1,000 mg/dL, and at that level the triglycerides are the cause.
54.explain:
## How fat injures the pancreas
The pancreas makes lipase. When blood loaded with chylomicrons passes through pancreatic capillaries, lipase leaking from acinar cells splits the triglycerides into free fatty acids. Normally albumin binds fatty acids, but here the amount overwhelms it, and unbound fatty acids are directly toxic to acinar cells and capillary endothelium. The chylomicrons also thicken the blood and plug capillaries, adding ischaemia. Injury releases more lipase, and the cycle continues.

## The numbers and the patients
Your causes card gives the threshold: causal above 1,000 mg/dL (about 11.3 mmol/L). Hypertriglyceridaemia is usually ranked the third commonest cause after gallstones and alcohol. It is almost always a genetic tendency (familial types I, IV and V) plus a trigger: uncontrolled diabetes, alcohol, pregnancy, oestrogens, hypothyroidism, or drugs. In the ICU remember propofol infusion as a trigger.

## Laboratory traps
- Measure triglycerides early. They fall quickly once the patient is fasting, so a late sample may miss the diagnosis.
- Lipaemic serum interferes with the amylase assay, so amylase can be falsely normal; lipase is more reliable.
- Sodium can read falsely low (pseudohyponatraemia) because fat displaces water in the sample.

## Treatment beyond standard care
Fluids, analgesia and early feeding are as for any pancreatitis. In addition the triglycerides are brought down, aiming for below 500 mg/dL:

- Intravenous insulin infusion with glucose as needed. Insulin activates lipoprotein lipase, the enzyme that clears chylomicrons, and is first choice, especially when glucose is high.
- Plasma exchange removes triglycerides quickly and is considered in severe cases with organ failure or when insulin fails; it has not been shown to improve survival.
- Heparin releases lipoprotein lipase but then depletes it, with rebound, so it is not used alone.
- After recovery: fibrates, a low-fat diet, alcohol abstinence and control of diabetes to prevent recurrence.

options.A: Alcohol can cause lipaemic serum, but the triglyceride rise is usually moderate and inconsistent; markedly raised levels indicate a lipid disorder as the cause.
options.B: Correct. Markedly raised triglycerides with lactescent serum identify hypertriglyceridaemic (hyperlipoproteinaemic) pancreatitis.
options.C: Drug-induced pancreatitis has no characteristic lipid finding, although a few drugs act by raising triglycerides.
options.D: Autoimmune pancreatitis is marked by raised IgG4 and a diffusely enlarged 'sausage' pancreas, not by lipids.

55.answer: B. Oral/rectal vancomycin plus IV metronidazole.
55.why: Hypotension, ileus and megacolon each define fulminant disease, and this patient has all three. The regimen is built around one problem: the drug has to reach the colonic lumen, and the gut has stopped moving. Vancomycin is not absorbed and works only by contact, so it is given at high dose by mouth or nasogastric tube and, because of the ileus, also as a retention enema from below. Intravenous metronidazole is added because it reaches the colon through the bloodstream and bile, independent of transit.
55.watch: Intravenous vancomycin is the classic distractor in other versions of this question: it does not cross into the colonic lumen and has no effect on C. difficile. Here the equivalent error is oral vancomycin alone, which pools above the ileus.
55.hook: With ileus, attack the colon from three directions: vancomycin from above, vancomycin from below, metronidazole through the blood.
55.explain:
## What to add to your treatment card
Your IDSA card has the regimen and the criteria. The details that turn it into answers are these.

The oral vancomycin dose rises from 125 mg to 500 mg four times daily in fulminant disease. Rectal vancomycin is 500 mg in about 100 mL of saline as a retention enema every six hours (IDSA). This bank's explanation quotes 500 mL; recognise either, but the guideline volume is 100 mL. Metronidazole is 500 mg intravenously every eight hours. This is the one setting where metronidazole is still required; it has otherwise been dropped to an alternative for mild disease only.

Fidaxomicin is preferred over vancomycin for non-severe and severe episodes because of fewer recurrences, but it has not been studied in fulminant disease and is not the recommended agent there.

Surgery should be discussed early, not after medical therapy has failed for days. A requirement for vasopressors, rising lactate, a very high white count, peritonitis or progressive dilatation are the usual triggers. The operations are subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy, or the colon-sparing alternative of a diverting loop ileostomy with colonic lavage.

options.A: Metronidazole alone is inferior even in mild disease. In fulminant colitis vancomycin in the lumen is the core of treatment.
options.B: Correct. High-dose enteral vancomycin, rectal vancomycin for the ileus, and intravenous metronidazole.
options.C: Fidaxomicin is first choice in non-fulminant infection but is unstudied in fulminant disease, and an oral-only drug will not pass an ileus.
options.D: Oral vancomycin cannot reach the colon reliably through an ileus, so on its own it is inadequate here.

56.answer: A. Radionuclide scan (technetium-99m labelled red cell scintigraphy).
56.why: The stem is built entirely around one number: 0.2 mL/min. Among the tests offered, only labelled red cell scintigraphy reliably detects bleeding that slow — it picks up rates of about 0.1 mL/min (some series as low as 0.05), where CT angiography needs about 0.3-0.5 mL/min and catheter angiography around 0.5-1 mL/min. It is also the only one of the four that tolerates an unprepared bowel and can be repeated over hours, which matters because obscure GI bleeding is usually intermittent.
56.watch: Capsule endoscopy is the right answer to a different question: obscure overt bleeding in a stable outpatient after negative upper and lower endoscopy, looked for over days. In an actively bleeding ICU patient it gives no real-time localisation and no treatment option, and a slow transit means the answer may arrive long after the decision is needed.
56.hook: Match the test to the bleeding rate: scintigraphy sees the slowest bleed, CT angiography needs a faster one, and catheter angiography needs faster still but can treat what it finds.
56.explain:
## Why bleeding rate decides the test
Every localising test for GI bleeding needs blood to actually leave the vessel while the test is running. The three imaging options differ in how much extravasated blood they need to show a signal.

- **Labelled red cell scintigraphy**: the patient's own red cells are tagged with technetium-99m and reinjected. Because the tracer stays in the circulation for hours, the gamma camera can be re-imaged repeatedly, and activity accumulating anywhere in the gut lumen is abnormal. This is the most sensitive of the three, detecting about 0.1 mL/min (the figure GT 8 asks directly), and it needs no bowel preparation and no contrast.
- **CT angiography**: fast, widely available, and anatomically precise — it shows contrast extravasating into the lumen and often the culprit lesion itself. It needs a brisker bleed, in the region of 0.3-0.5 mL/min, and it costs a contrast load in a patient who may need the kidneys later.
- **Catheter (mesenteric) angiography**: the least sensitive, needing roughly 0.5-1 mL/min, but the only one that treats — superselective embolisation at the same sitting.

## The trade-off the examiner wants
Scintigraphy's weakness is the mirror of its strength. It is sensitive but imprecise: tracer tracks along the bowel, so it localises to a region of the abdomen rather than to a vessel, and false localisation is common. It also gives no therapy. So it earns its place as a screening or triage test — a positive scan tells you bleeding is active now and justifies moving to angiography, while a negative scan in a stable patient supports watching.

## Neighbouring facts worth holding
- Hematochezia with haemodynamic instability should raise suspicion of a brisk **upper** GI source: up to about 15% of apparent lower GI bleeds come from above the ligament of Treitz, which is why upper endoscopy comes first in that setting.
- In practice, current gastroenterology guidance for haemodynamically significant ongoing hematochezia favours going straight to **CT angiography** followed by angiographic treatment, precisely because speed and the ability to treat matter more than sensitivity when the bleed is fast. Scintigraphy is the answer when the bleed is slow, intermittent, and obscure — exactly as this stem is worded.
- Colonoscopy remains the diagnostic standard in the stable patient, but it needs purge preparation, which this stem has explicitly removed from the table.
- Small bowel sources (angioectasia, Dieulafoy lesion, Meckel's diverticulum, NSAID ulceration) dominate the obscure group; a Meckel's scan uses technetium pertechnetate to image ectopic gastric mucosa, which is a different scan from a labelled red cell study.

options.A: Correct. The most sensitive of the four for slow bleeding (about 0.1 mL/min), needs no bowel preparation, and can be reimaged over hours to catch an intermittent bleed.
options.B: CT angiography generally needs about 0.3-0.5 mL/min. At the stated 0.2 mL/min it is likely to be negative, even though in a fast bleed it would be the first test.
options.C: Catheter angiography is the least sensitive, needing roughly 0.5-1 mL/min. Its value is treatment, so it follows a positive localising study rather than leading.
options.D: Capsule endoscopy is for obscure bleeding in a stable patient once active bleeding has settled. It gives no immediate localisation, no therapy, and the read may come too late to act on.

56.picks_note: HT picked D, which is the standard answer to "endoscopy negative, where is the bleed?" — but that is the elective version of the question. This patient is bleeding now, in the ICU, and the stem supplies a rate specifically so you choose on sensitivity rather than on completeness of mucosal survey.

key.note: The key follows standard texts. Note the real-world divergence: for haemodynamically significant ongoing hematochezia, current ACG guidance starts with CT angiography; the stem's slow rate and unsafe bowel preparation are what make scintigraphy the intended answer.

57.why: The stem has already excluded the two defects that get blamed first: the platelet count is adequate and the factor levels are normal. What temperature still takes away at 33 degrees is platelet function rather than platelet number. Cooling impairs the von Willebrand factor-GPIb interaction and platelet activation, so platelets reach the exposed subendothelium but stick and spread poorly, and primary haemostasis fails as diffuse microvascular oozing.
57.watch: The tempting answer is to call it a cascade problem, because hypothermia does slow every enzyme. But enzyme activity falls meaningfully only below about 33 degrees, and the stem states the factor levels are normal; a laboratory factor level is measured in a warm analyser and therefore cannot show you the temperature-dependent loss anyway.
57.hook: At mild hypothermia the clot fails at the platelet, not at the enzyme: 33 degrees buys you a platelet function defect with a normal platelet count and normal factor levels.
57.explain:
## What temperature does, in order
Cooling hits haemostasis in a sequence, and knowing the sequence answers most questions on this topic.

**Mild hypothermia, roughly 37 down to 34 degrees.** Platelet function is the first casualty. Platelet adhesion and aggregation are measurably reduced at 33 degrees compared with 37, while thrombin generation is still largely preserved. Mechanistically, cold reduces GPIb-mediated binding to von Willebrand factor, blunts activation and shape change, impairs thromboxane A2 generation, and causes reversible sequestration of platelets in the liver and spleen. The clinical signature is exactly what the stem describes: generalised oozing from cut surfaces, puncture sites and mucosa, with a count and a coagulation screen that look acceptable.

**Below about 33 degrees.** Now the enzymes join in. Coagulation factor enzymatic activity falls progressively as temperature drops, so clot initiation and propagation slow as well; by deep hypothermia both arms are severely impaired.

## Why the laboratory lies to you
PT, aPTT and factor assays are run at 37 degrees. A hypothermic bleeding patient can therefore have a normal screen while bleeding from a defect that only exists at the patient's actual temperature. Viscoelastic testing has the same limitation unless the cartridge is run at the patient's temperature. The practical consequence is that rewarming is a haemostatic intervention, not just supportive care, and in a cold bleeding trauma patient it comes before escalating product.

## The neighbouring facts an examiner can reach for
- The lethal triad is hypothermia, acidosis and coagulopathy, each aggravating the others; your trauma card carries the thresholds and the odds ratios.
- Acidosis is the complementary insult: lowering pH from 7.4 to 7.0 cuts factor VIIa activity by over 90% and tissue factor-VIIa activity by over 60%, and the Xa-Va complex is impaired as well; correcting pH with bicarbonate alone does not restore coagulation.
- Early trauma-induced coagulopathy is a different mechanism again - shock-driven protein C activation and hyperfibrinolysis, with fibrinogen falling first - and it is present on arrival, before any cold fluid.
- Management therefore runs in parallel: active rewarming and warmed products and fluid, calcium, tranexamic acid within 3 hours, fibrinogen replacement, and surgical control. Transfused product cannot outrun a core temperature of 33 degrees.

options.A: Hyperfibrinolysis is central to early trauma-induced coagulopathy from shock, but it is not what mild hypothermia itself produces, and the stem gives no sign of lysis.
options.B: Correct. Cold impairs platelet adhesion and activation at temperatures that still leave thrombin generation and factor levels intact, which fits a normal count and normal factor levels with diffuse oozing.
options.C: Backwards. Cooling slows enzymatic reactions, so thrombin generation is reduced or at best unchanged, never increased.
options.D: Excess tissue factor would drive consumptive coagulopathy with falling fibrinogen and platelets. The stem's normal values argue against it, and it is not a temperature effect.

58.why: Nothing in this stem is a contraindication to enteral nutrition. Severe pancreatitis is not an indication for bowel rest, absent bowel sounds and gastric atony are motility findings rather than evidence of a non-functioning absorptive surface, and distension is minimal with no obstruction. What the gastric atony does tell you is that the stomach will not empty reliably, so the tube tip goes beyond the pylorus and uses the small bowel that is still working.
58.watch: The trap is treating flatus or bowel sounds as the licence to feed. Both are colonic and gastric motility signs with poor correlation to small intestinal absorption, and waiting for them simply accumulates a calorie and protein deficit. Parenteral nutrition is the answer only when the gut is unusable, inaccessible or insufficient, and here it is none of those.
58.hook: Gastric atony changes the route, not the decision: feed past the pylorus rather than switching to a vein or to nothing.
58.explain:
## Why the gut still gets fed
Your enteral access and contraindication cards carry the lists; the point to add here is the reasoning behind them. The absolute contraindications are all states where feeding would either be unsafe or useless - uncontrolled shock, bowel ischaemia, obstruction or perforation, abdominal compartment syndrome. Ileus and gastroparesis sit in neither of those categories: the mucosa is perfused and absorbing, only motility has failed. Enteral feed maintains enterocyte nutrition and the mucosal barrier, and in severe acute pancreatitis specifically it produces fewer infectious complications than parenteral nutrition.

## Choosing the route
Nasogastric is the default and, in pancreatitis, is as effective as nasojejunal when it is tolerated - it does not provoke the disease by stimulating the pancreas, which is the old misconception behind bowel rest. Postpyloric feeding is for the patient in whom gastric delivery fails: high residuals or vomiting despite a prokinetic, or clear gastric atony as here. Feeding past the pylorus also reduces aspiration risk somewhat, which is a bonus rather than the reason.

## Two numbers to keep
Start enteral nutrition within 24-48 hours of ICU admission once haemodynamically stable, and accept hypocaloric delivery in the first week; your feeding card has the targets. If enteral delivery stays inadequate, supplemental parenteral nutrition is weighed case by case during the first week (ESPEN) and, by ASPEN, only after about 7-10 days - never on day one of an ileus.

options.A: Correct. The small bowel is working; the stomach is not. Postpyloric delivery bypasses the one failed step and keeps the gut fed.
options.B: Parenteral nutrition is for a gut that cannot be used or cannot meet needs. Starting it here adds line infection, hyperglycaemia and liver risk for no gain, and in severe pancreatitis it increases infectious complications relative to enteral feeding.
options.C: Flatus and bowel sounds are poor surrogates for small bowel absorption. Waiting for them delays nutrition without making it safer.
options.D: Routine bowel rest in acute pancreatitis is obsolete. Prolonged fasting worsens gut barrier function and accrues a nutritional deficit.

59.answer: B. Reduce glucose and fat (cut total calories).
59.why: An RQ of 1.08 is a total-calorie signal, not a substrate signal. Respiratory quotient is CO2 produced divided by O2 consumed; oxidising fat gives about 0.7, mixed substrate about 0.8, pure carbohydrate 1.0, and anything above 1.0 means carbon is being converted into fat, which generates CO2 without consuming proportionate oxygen. Net lipogenesis only happens when energy delivery exceeds expenditure, so the appropriate intervention is to lower the total prescription and re-measure, not to shuffle calories between glucose and lipid.
59.watch: Replacing glucose with lipid is the attractive wrong answer because carbohydrate has the higher RQ. It lowers the RQ figure slightly while the patient remains overfed: total calories, and therefore CO2 production and ventilatory load, are essentially unchanged, and high lipid loads add hypertriglyceridaemia.
59.hook: An RQ above 1.0 in a hypercapnic patient on nutrition is a verdict on the total, not on the mix: cut the calories.
59.explain:
## Reading the number
The values worth knowing cold: fat 0.7, protein about 0.8, mixed substrate 0.8-0.85, carbohydrate 1.0, net lipogenesis above 1.0, and a physiologically implausible value below about 0.65 or above about 1.3 usually means a leak, a chest drain, an air leak around the cuff or an unsteady state rather than real metabolism.

In this patient the chain runs: excess calories, net lipogenesis, more CO2 produced per unit oxygen consumed, higher minute ventilation demanded to clear it. In a COPD patient with limited ventilatory reserve, that extra CO2 load shows up as rising PaCO2 and failure to wean, with pulmonary mechanics unchanged because the lung has not changed - the metabolic load has.

## What to do and what else is hidden
Reduce total energy delivery, then reassess with calorimetry. Remember the calories that are not on the feed chart: propofol carries about 1.1 kcal/mL as lipid, dextrose-containing infusions and citrate anticoagulation add more. Hunting those is often the quickest way to fix an overfed patient. One honest caveat for the exam: RQ is a crude detector of overfeeding in practice, which is why the measured energy expenditure, not the RQ alone, drives the prescription - but an RQ above 1.0 with unexplained hypercapnia is still the classic examined pattern.

options.A: More protein does nothing about a calorie excess and adds urea load; protein dosing is decided separately from this problem.
options.B: Correct. An RQ above 1.0 means net lipogenesis from overfeeding, so total energy delivery comes down and is then rechecked by calorimetry.
options.C: Swapping the high-RQ substrate for the low-RQ one changes the number more than the patient, leaves the calorie excess in place, and risks hypertriglyceridaemia.
options.D: Branched-chain amino acids have no role in overfeeding-related CO2 production and no consistent ICU outcome benefit.

59.picks_note: Your pick, C, is the right physiology aimed at the wrong target - lipid does have a lower RQ, so substituting it lowers the measured ratio. But the RQ was only the clue; the disease is the total calorie load, and swapping substrates leaves CO2 production and ventilatory demand where they were.

60.why: In the cell-based model, factor VIIIa and factor IXa assemble on the activated platelet membrane to form intrinsic tenase, and that complex is the main generator of factor Xa during propagation. The small amount of thrombin made during initiation exists mainly to create this machinery: it activates platelets, cleaves factor VIII from von Willebrand factor to make VIIIa, and activates factor XI, which supplies more IXa. Propagation is therefore defined by the FVIIIa/FIXa complex, and this is why haemophilia bleeds despite intact initiation.
60.watch: Initiation also makes factor Xa, which makes it a plausible answer, but it does so through tissue factor-FVIIa (extrinsic tenase) on tissue factor-bearing cells, not through VIIIa/FIXa, and only in trace quantities. The question asks which step depends on the intrinsic tenase complex, and that is propagation.
60.hook: Initiation makes the spark with tissue factor-FVIIa; propagation makes the fire with FVIIIa/FIXa on the platelet surface.
60.explain:
## The cell-based model in three phases
The old cascade with separate intrinsic and extrinsic arms explains the laboratory tests but not the patient. The cell-based model replaces it with phases that happen on specific cell surfaces.

**Initiation.** Vessel injury exposes tissue factor on subendothelial cells. Tissue factor binds factor VIIa to form extrinsic tenase, which activates factors X and IX. The Xa generated here, with Va, makes a trace of thrombin. Tissue factor pathway inhibitor shuts this step down quickly, so initiation alone can never produce enough thrombin to make a clot.

**Amplification.** That trace of thrombin works on surfaces rather than on fibrinogen. It fully activates platelets, which expose phosphatidylserine and bind the factors; it releases factor VIII from von Willebrand factor and activates it to VIIIa; it activates factor V to Va and factor XI to XIa.

**Propagation.** On the activated platelet surface, VIIIa and IXa form intrinsic tenase, which activates factor X far more efficiently than tissue factor-FVIIa could, and Xa with Va forms prothrombinase, which converts prothrombin to thrombin at an enormously accelerated rate. The result is the thrombin burst that converts fibrinogen to fibrin, activates factor XIII for cross-linking, and makes a clot that holds.

## Why this model earns its place in the exam
- It explains haemophilia A and B: initiation is normal, so the PT is normal, but without VIIIa or IXa there is no intrinsic tenase, the burst never comes, and a clot forms and then falls apart - hence delayed bleeding and haemarthroses.
- It explains why recombinant factor VIIa can work in haemophilia with inhibitors: in supraphysiological doses it generates Xa directly on the platelet surface and bypasses the missing complex.
- It explains the amplifying power of the complexes: factor Xa assembled with Va on a phospholipid surface activates prothrombin orders of magnitude faster than free Xa, which is why calcium and an intact platelet membrane are not optional extras in a bleeding patient.
- In trauma, this is the model behind giving calcium, keeping the patient warm and replacing fibrinogen: the surfaces, cofactors and substrate all have to be present for propagation to happen.

options.A: Initiation runs on tissue factor-bearing cells through tissue factor-FVIIa, and produces only trace thrombin. It does not depend on FVIIIa/FIXa.
options.B: Fibrinolysis is plasmin degrading formed fibrin, downstream of everything the question is about.
options.C: Correct. FVIIIa/FIXa (intrinsic tenase) on the activated platelet surface drives factor X activation during propagation and so drives the thrombin burst.
options.D: Platelet adhesion is primary haemostasis, mediated by von Willebrand factor, GPIb and collagen. It positions the surface on which propagation later occurs, but it does not need VIIIa/IXa.

60.picks_note: HT picked A, which is where the logic lands if the question is read as "where does coagulation begin?" Initiation is indeed the first appearance of Xa and thrombin, but it is tissue factor-FVIIa that does it; the stem names FVIIIa/FIXa specifically, and that complex only exists after amplification, on the platelet surface.

61.why: The question asks for the typical value, which is a measure of central tendency, and the distribution is right-skewed by a single 150-day stay. The mean is computed from the magnitudes of all observations, so one extreme value drags it away from where most patients actually sit. The median depends only on rank, so an outlier moves it by at most one position. That resistance is precisely why length of stay, duration of ventilation and cost are reported as medians with interquartile range.
61.watch: Standard deviation and range are the distractors that answer a different question: both describe spread, not the typical patient, and both are at least as outlier-sensitive as the mean. If a stem asks for the typical or representative value, only mean, median and mode are in the running.
61.hook: Skewed data, long tail, one monstrous outlier: report the median with an interquartile range, because the mean describes a patient who does not exist.
61.explain:
## Why the mean fails here
The mean uses every value's size, so adding one 150-day stay to a cohort of ordinary stays adds that whole excess, divided by n, to the average. In a right-skewed distribution the order becomes mean greater than median greater than mode - your skew card has this - so the mean overstates the typical stay. The median is the middle value after ranking, and swapping an extreme value for a merely large one does not change the ranking of the middle observation at all.

## What to pair the median with, and what to test with
- Report the median with the **interquartile range**, not with the standard deviation; the SD belongs to the mean and to roughly symmetric data.
- Skewed data push you towards **non-parametric tests**: Mann-Whitney U for two independent groups, Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired data, Kruskal-Wallis for three or more.
- An alternative to discarding the mean is to transform: log-transforming right-skewed data often restores approximate normality, and the geometric mean is the back-transformed average.
- The mode is the most frequent value and is rarely the examined answer for continuous data, though it is the only usable central measure for nominal data.

options.A: Correct. The median is rank-based and so is minimally affected by the 150-day outlier, making it the representative value for a skewed stay distribution.
options.B: The mean uses the size of every observation and is pulled upward by a single very long stay, so it overstates the typical patient in a right-skewed distribution.
options.C: Standard deviation measures dispersion around the mean. It does not name a typical value, and it is inflated by the same outlier.
options.D: Range is minimum to maximum and is defined entirely by the two most extreme observations - the worst possible choice when an outlier is present.

61.picks_note: Your pick, B, is the default answer to "what is the average stay?" and would be correct for a symmetric distribution. The stem specifically plants the word skewed and a 150-day outlier, which is the examiner signalling that the mean has been contaminated and the rank-based measure is wanted.

62.why: RASS runs from -5 to +4 and the values have a genuine order, from unrousable through calm to combative, so it is not nominal. But the steps are not equal quantities: the distance from -5 to -4 is not the same amount of sedation as the distance from 0 to +1, and there is no unit of sedation being measured. Order without equal intervals is the definition of an ordinal scale, and the investigators' assumption of equal intervals is the error the stem is pointing at, not a reason to reclassify the variable.
62.watch: Read the stem carefully: the investigators assume equal intervals, and the question asks what the variable actually is. Treating ordinal scores as interval data is what licenses means and parametric tests on them, and it is a common and criticised practice with RASS, GCS, pain scores and NYHA class.
62.hook: A number with an order but no fixed step size is ordinal, however much the analysis plan wishes it were continuous.
62.explain:
## The four scales, and where RASS sits
Your data-scales card carries the table; the distinctions that get examined are these. **Nominal** data are named categories with no order - blood group, organism, mode of ventilation. **Ordinal** data have an inherent order but unequal or unknown gaps - ASA grade, NYHA class, AGI grade, RASS, GCS, Likert responses. **Interval** data have equal gaps but no absolute zero - temperature in degrees Celsius. **Ratio** data have equal gaps and a true zero, so ratios are meaningful - sodium, weight, FEV1, cardiac output.

## Why the classification changes the analysis
The scale decides what you may legitimately calculate and which test you may run.

- Ordinal data are summarised by median and interquartile range, or by proportions in each category; a mean RASS of -1.7 is reported often and defensible only loosely.
- Ordinal data go to non-parametric tests: Mann-Whitney U or Wilcoxon rank sum for two independent groups, Wilcoxon signed-rank for paired, Kruskal-Wallis for three or more, Spearman rho for correlation, and ordinal logistic regression when the score is the outcome.
- Dichotomous is a special case of nominal with exactly two categories, which is what you create when you collapse RASS into "adequately sedated or not" - a legitimate move that then sends you to chi-square or logistic regression.
- Collapsing an ordinal scale into two groups costs information and statistical power, which is the trade-off the exam likes to ask about.

options.A: Nominal means unordered categories. RASS values have a clear clinical order from deep sedation to agitation, so this fails.
options.B: Correct. RASS has rank order without equal or measurable intervals, which is exactly an ordinal scale.
options.C: Continuous data can take any value on a scale with equal intervals. RASS takes fixed integer categories whose spacing has no defined quantity.
options.D: Dichotomous means two categories only. RASS has ten levels; dichotomising it is an analytic choice, not what the variable is.

key.note: DocT's explanation uses RASS as its worked ordinal example. The stem's clause about assuming equal intervals is muddled wording; the answer is ordinal regardless.

64.why: One-way ANOVA treats its groups as independent samples. Here the four PaO2 values at baseline, 6, 12 and 24 hours come from the same patients, so a patient with poor oxygenation at baseline is likely to be low at every later time point. That within-patient correlation breaks the independence assumption, which inflates the error term and makes the test invalid rather than merely imprecise. Repeated-measures ANOVA, or a mixed-effects model, partitions out the between-subject variation and analyses the within-subject change.
64.watch: Non-normality and unequal group sizes are real ANOVA concerns, which is what makes them tempting; the distinction is that both are assumption violations ANOVA can often tolerate or be corrected for, while dependence between observations is structural and cannot be patched. If the same patients appear in every column, no amount of normality rescues one-way ANOVA.
64.hook: Ask first whether the data are paired: same patients measured again means a repeated-measures design, and one-way ANOVA is the wrong tool before you check anything else.
64.explain:
## The two questions that pick the test
Your test-selection card puts it as data type, then number and pairing of groups. This item is the second question. Independent groups measured once go to unpaired t-test (two groups) or one-way ANOVA (three or more). The same subjects measured repeatedly go to paired t-test (two time points) or repeated-measures ANOVA (three or more), with Friedman's test as the non-parametric equivalent and Kruskal-Wallis as the non-parametric version of the one-way, independent-groups case.

## Why dependence matters mechanically
ANOVA compares variability between groups with variability within groups. When each subject contributes to every group, part of the within-group variability is just stable differences between patients, which has nothing to do with time. Leaving it in the error term usually makes the test conservative and wastes the design's main advantage - each patient acts as his own control. Repeated-measures ANOVA removes that between-subject component, which is why it is more powerful for the same n.

## Two extras worth holding
- Repeated-measures ANOVA adds its own assumption, **sphericity**: the variances of the differences between all pairs of time points should be equal. When it is violated, a Greenhouse-Geisser or Huynh-Feldt correction is applied.
- A significant overall result tells you only that the time points differ somewhere, so post-hoc pairwise comparisons with correction for multiple testing (Bonferroni, Tukey) follow. Mixed-effects models are now preferred when data are missing at some time points, because repeated-measures ANOVA discards any patient with an incomplete set.

options.A: Non-normality is an ANOVA assumption too, but it is addressable by transformation or a non-parametric test, and it is not what the repeated-measures design violates.
options.B: Unequal group sizes are tolerated by ANOVA with only modest effect on robustness, and in a repeated-measures design every time point has the same patients anyway.
options.C: Correct. Measurements from the same patient are correlated, which violates the independence assumption; repeated-measures ANOVA or a mixed model accounts for it.
options.D: High variance widens confidence intervals and reduces power but breaks no assumption; it does not make the analysis inappropriate.

64.picks_note: HT picked D, treating scatter as the problem. Variance is what ANOVA is built to analyse; the fault the stem plants is structural - four values per patient, so the observations are not independent of each other.

65.answer: B. Give plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate.
65.why: R time is the interval from the start of the test until the trace first shows measurable clot, so it reports how quickly thrombin generation gets going - a clotting factor function. Prolonged R with a normal alpha angle, normal MA and negligible LY30 isolates the defect to initiation: fibrinogen is adequate, platelet-dependent clot strength is adequate, and there is no hyperfibrinolysis. The targeted replacement is therefore coagulation factors, as plasma or as prothrombin complex concentrate.
65.watch: The trap is reflex trauma management: a bleeding trauma patient gets platelets, cryoprecipitate and tranexamic acid, so all three distractors feel right. The whole purpose of a viscoelastic trace is to stop that reflex - each parameter maps to one product, and the normal MA, normal alpha angle and flat LY30 here specifically exclude the other three.
65.hook: Read the trace parameter by parameter: R is factors, alpha angle is fibrinogen, MA is platelets, LY30 is lysis - and give only what the abnormal parameter asks for.
65.explain:
## The four numbers and what each one owns
A kaolin-activated TEG gives four parameters that matter at the bedside, and each has one dominant determinant.

- **R time** (reaction time, roughly 4-8 minutes): time to the start of clot formation. Driven by **clotting factor activity**. Prolonged by factor deficiency or dilution, by vitamin K antagonists, and by heparin. Treat with plasma or prothrombin complex concentrate; if heparin is the cause, protamine.
- **K time and alpha angle** (alpha roughly 47-74 degrees): how fast the clot gains strength. Driven mainly by **fibrinogen**, with a platelet contribution. Low alpha angle means cryoprecipitate or fibrinogen concentrate.
- **MA** (maximum amplitude, roughly 55-73 mm): peak clot strength. Driven mainly by **platelet number and function**, with a fibrinogen contribution. Low MA means platelets, with desmopressin considered if the count is adequate but function is not.
- **LY30** (percentage lysis 30 minutes after MA, normally under about 8%): clot breakdown. Raised means hyperfibrinolysis and calls for tranexamic acid.

Exact reference ranges differ between devices and between native and activated assays, so the pattern matters more than the decimal.

## Translating to ROTEM, and the practical caveats
Your ROTEM card maps the same logic with different names: R corresponds to CT, alpha angle and K to CFT, MA to MCF, LY30 to maximum lysis. ROTEM's advantage is its channels - EXTEM for the extrinsic side, INTEM for the intrinsic, HEPTEM adding heparinase to reveal heparin effect, FIBTEM blocking platelets to isolate fibrinogen.

Two caveats that are themselves examinable. First, these assays run at 37 degrees unless the device is set otherwise, so they underestimate the coagulopathy of a hypothermic patient.
